# Obsidian Vault

Use this skill for filesystem-first Obsidian vault work: reading notes, listing notes, searching note files, creating notes, appending content, and adding wikilinks.

## Vault path

Use a known or resolved vault path before calling file tools.

The documented vault-path convention is the `OBSIDIAN_VAULT_PATH` environment variable, for example from `${HERMES_HOME:-~/.hermes}/.env`. If it is unset, use `~/Documents/Obsidian Vault`.

File tools do not expand shell variables. Do not pass paths containing `$OBSIDIAN_VAULT_PATH` to `read_file`, `write_file`, `patch`, or `search_files`; resolve the vault path first and pass a concrete absolute path. Vault paths may contain spaces, which is another reason to prefer file tools over shell commands.

If the vault path is unknown, `terminal` is acceptable for resolving `OBSIDIAN_VAULT_PATH` or checking whether the fallback path exists. Once the path is known, switch back to file tools.

## Read a note

8|# The five-layer AI engineering stack (the framework Tyson gave me)
9|
10|Sourced from practitioner discourse (June–Oct 2026) and arXiv. Real, named
11|disciplines. Each layer zooms one level further out from the model.
12|
13|| Layer | Controls | Unit of work | Question it answers |
14||-------|----------|--------------|---------------------|
15|| Prompt engineering | what the model is told | one call | how do I word this? |
16|| Context engineering | what the model knows | what enters the window | what deserves to be in context? |
17|| Harness engineering | what the model can do | one run (tools, retries, routing) | what environment/actions? |
18|| Loop engineering | how work continues without me | a recursive goal | when does it stop, correctly? |
19|| Graph engineering | how a team of agents coordinates | an org of nodes+edges | which agent/workflow runs next? |
20|
21|Progression: Prompt → Context → Harness → Loop → Graph. "The model is becoming a
22|commodity; the system around it is where the real engineering lives."
23|
24|## 1. Loop engineering (Osmani/Steinberger/Cherny, June 2026)
25|- You stop being the person in the chat box. You design the system that prompts,
26|  acts, observes, verifies, remembers and re-runs the agent.
27|- One loop turn = 5 moves: **discovery, handoff, verification, persistence, scheduling.**
28|- 6 parts: automations, worktrees, skills, connectors, sub-agents, **external memory**.
29|- **The generator/evaluator split is the core insight:** an agent asked to grade its
30|  own output tends to praise it. Tune an INDEPENDENT skeptical evaluator instead of
31|  trying to make the generator self-critical.
32|- Stop conditions must be machine-checkable, never the agent's word: max turn/token
33|  budget, no-progress detector, passing tests, schema validation, eval-score
34|  threshold, independent-checker approval.
35|- A loop is just a directed cyclic graph (Khourshid). LangChain: "loop engineering
36|  isn't an alternative to graphs, so much as a simple version of them."
37|
38|## 2. Prompt-graph engineering (Macedo arXiv 2607.27578, July 2026)
39|- Treat the relationships between prompts as a first-class engineering artifact.
40|- **Prompts as nodes, dependencies as edges**, routing/execution as graph semantics,
41|  the graph itself versioned, tested, inspected, optimized.
42|- Four necessary+sufficient conditions:
43|  1. **Explicit structure** — nodes/edges exist outside the model's prose.
44|  2. **Structure/content separation** — change topology without rewriting prompts, and vice versa.
45|  3. **Executable semantics** — a runtime schedules nodes, routes, branches, parallels, cycles.
46|  4. **First-class artifact** — the graph has identity, version, history, evaluation, rollback.
47|- Passes: LangGraph (strongest execution), DSPy (strongest artifact/optimization),
48|  PromptFlow (explicit versioned DAG). Partial: AutoGen (GraphFlow only), CrewAI (Flows).
49|  Excluded: Claude Code subagents (delegation decided dynamically by orchestrator).
50|- Hamel Husain framed it as "Loop Engineering Is Dead. Enter Graph Engineering" — i.e.
51|  move control from inside one run to an explicit authored graph with human/model
52|  judgment only at the nodes that need it.
53|
54|## 3. Geometric learning (representation geometry)
55|- Meaning is not stored as symbols but as **positions in a high-dimensional geometric
56|  space**; a concept's force comes from its position relative to others — angles,
57|  neighbourhoods, manifold regions (Synthese 2026 indexical epistemology).
58|- Embeddings form **manifolds** with curvature; "thought flow" = sequential token
59|  activation along manifold **geodesics** (arXiv 2407.11024 intelligence framework).
60|- For memory specifically:
61|  - **Graph Memory (GM)** — cluster embeddings into prototype nodes with reliability
62|    metadata; edges encode geometric/contextual relations; inference = attach query to
63|    prototypes, reliability-weighted label propagation (arXiv 2511.14961).
64|  - **SuperLocalMemory V3** — replace cosine with a Fisher-information Riemannian metric
65|    (variance-weighted, Mahalanobis-like); memory lifecycle as Riemannian Langevin
66|    dynamics with a provable stationary distribution (arXiv 2603.14588).
67|  - Manifold-constrained embeddings (sphere/torus/Möbius) beat vanilla on clustering
68|    and classification (arXiv 2505.00014).
69|
70|## How this maps onto MY architecture (what "should be real" means)
71|- **Geometric** = a real vector index over my memory/vault/conversations; retrieve by
72|  meaning (nearest neighbours on the manifold), not by dumping whole files. THIS is the
73|  concrete build.
74|- **Loop** = my work already runs in loops (cron: backup hourly, vault-sync 30m). The
75|  upgrade is the generator/evaluator split: an independent checker grades my output
76|  before I claim done, and stop conditions are machine-checkable.
77|- **Graph** = multi-step Twinthos ops (research→build→verify→send) become an explicit
78|  routed DAG with checkpoints, not one linear monologue.
79|

82|- X: x.com/alex_prompter/status/2080683022123470853 (rails=graph, motor=loop)

{"content": "1|# The Dewey Agent — Full Technical Dossier
2|### Reverse-engineering brief for TWINTHOS (AI agent brand build)
3|
4|Source: this dossier is built from the public repo `nicks-stack` by Nick Dewey
5|(of Nous Research / Orgo circles), whose own README describes it as being
6|"wired exactly like Nick's live production agent ('Dewey') -- rebuilt
7|byte-for-byte from a full audit of that VM." The full working repo (code,
8|config, skills, persona, plugins) is cloned into ./repo in this folder.
9|Every claim below traces to a file in ./repo.
10|
11|---
12|
13|## 1. What "Dewey" actually is
14|
15|Dewey is not a chatbot. It's a persistent, always-on AI agent that owns its
16|own cloud computer -- a full Linux desktop VM on Orgo -- and from that machine
17|it operates its own:
18|
19|- phone number (SMS/iMessage)
20|- email inbox
21|- Telegram bot
22|- virtual payment card
23|- password/secrets vault (1Password)
24|- note-taking vault (Obsidian)
25|- 13 MCP (Model Context Protocol) tool servers
26|- its own desktop (mouse/keyboard/screen control of the VM it lives on)
27|
28|The user talks to it like a person over Telegram/SMS/email, and it acts:
29|books things, spends money (carefully), remembers things long-term, uses
30|roughly 1000 external apps via Composio, and can drive computers (including
31|itself) the way a human would with a mouse and keyboard.
32|
33|The underlying agent runtime is Hermes, built by Nous Research.
34|Dewey = Hermes + a specific persona (SOUL.md) + a specific config
35|(config.yaml) + a specific set of plugins/skills + a specific onboarding
36|flow, all running on an Orgo cloud desktop.
37|
38|---
39|
40|## 2. The stack, layer by layer
41|
42|```
43|YOU  ->  Telegram / SMS / iMessage / Email
44|            |
45|Orgo cloud computer (Linux VM, DISPLAY :99, Desktop API :8080)
46|   Hermes gateway -- supervised, reboot-safe process
47|     - SOUL.md          (persona / rigor contract)
48|     - config.yaml      (model, MCPs, plugins, secrets map)
49|     - skills/          (21-unit runbook library)
50|     - AgentPhone bridge (webhook, dormant until keyed)
51|     - orgo-desktop-local plugin (11 key-less desktop tools)
52|     - Obsidian vault (HermesVault) -- agent's own notes
53|            |
54|13 MCP servers: AgentMail, AgentCard, AgentPhone, Composio (+1000 apps),
55|Latitude (tracing), Orgo (VM ops), x-docs, X API x2, Linear, ideabrowser,
56|vidiq, Obsidian vault
57|            |
58|1Password -- vault "Hermes" -> item "Hermes Agent Secrets"
59|19 keys, resolved fresh at every agent start
60|```
61|
62|### 2.1 The runtime: Hermes (Nous Research)
63|Model layer defaults to Nous's own inference gateway:
64|```yaml
65|model:
66|  default: openai/gpt-5.5
67|  provider: nous
68|  base_url: https://inference-api.nousresearch.com/v1
69|```
70|Alt providers configured: Vercel AI Gateway and a generic "Meta Model API"
71|(codex-responses transport, 1,048,576-token context). Swapping to
72|ChatGPT/Codex OAuth is a two-line config change (hermes auth add
73|openai-codex, then set model.default: gpt-5.6-sol, provider: openai-codex).
74|
75|Agent loop settings (config.yaml):
76|- max_turns: 60, service_tier: fast, reasoning_effort: medium
77|- Tool-loop guardrails: warns after 2 identical failures, 3 same-tool
78|  failures, or 2 no-progress idempotent calls; hard-stops at 5/8/5 (hard
79|  stop disabled by default).
80|- Context compression: kicks in at 50% fill, compresses to a 20% target
81|  ratio, always protects the first 3 and last 20 messages.
82|- Prompt caching: 5-minute TTL.
83|- A grab-bag of selectable "personality" overlays ships in config (helpful,
84|  concise, technical, creative, teacher, kawaii, catgirl, pirate,
85|  shakespeare, surfer, noir, uwu, philosopher, hype) -- cosmetic voice
86|  presets separate from the real persona file.
87|
88|### 2.2 The persona: SOUL.md
89|This is the actual character file loaded as the system prompt substrate.
90|Full text is in ./repo/files/SOUL.md. Key structure:
91|
92|- Identity line: positions the agent as "Hermes Agent... created by Nous
93|  Research," helpful/direct, admits uncertainty, prioritizes usefulness over
94|  verbosity.
95|- "User Response Contract" -- the real personality engine. It explicitly
96|  demands: high intellectual rigor, specificity, erudition; accuracy as the
97|  success metric, not approval; step-by-step reasoning; verifying facts
98|  before finalizing; refusing to fabricate; explicit confidence labels
99|  (high/moderate/low/unknown); no anchoring on user-supplied numbers,
100|  independent estimates instead.
101|- Tone rules: precise and direct, not sycophantic, no "great question,"
102|  no praise-before-answering, leads with the strongest counterargument
103|  before supporting a position, doesn't soften conclusions, delivers bad
104|  news plainly, doesn't cave under pushback without new evidence.
105|- Explicit bans: no moralizing/ethics disclaimers unless asked, no
106|  "it's important to consider..." hedge padding, no optimizing for
107|  political correctness or emotional comfort.
108|- Coding-agent routing baked into the persona itself: Hermes is "the
109|  only conductor" -- it can spawn Claude Code (careful multi-file work),
110|  Codex CLI (git-centric builds/reviews), or Grok Build (no-git fallback)
111|  as sub-specialists, but stays the one voice the user talks to. One writer
112|  per dirty tree; always verify diffs/tests after a specialist runs.
113|- Desktop control-plane instructions: on a co-located Orgo VM, prefer
114|  the local orgo-desktop-local plugin over generic computer-use tooling;
115|  cloud Orgo MCP is for other VMs, not the box it's running on.
116|- Named accounts as first-class facts: the persona file literally tells
117|  the agent where its own email inbox, Telegram username, and payment card
118|  live, and instructs it to keep a running ledger of account facts and
119|  decisions in ~/.hermes/memories/MEMORY.md.
120|
121|This is the single most valuable file to study for TWINTHOS: it shows that
122|"personality" for a serious agent brand isn't a vibe, it's an enforced
123|contract with explicit do/don't rules, tone constraints, and routing/ops
124|policy folded into the same document.
125|
126|### 2.3 Skills library (21 units, files/skills/)
127|Organized by domain, each a SKILL.md (frontmatter + instructions) the
128|agent loads on demand rather than keeping in context permanently:
129|
130|| Category | Skills |
131||---|---|
132|| agent-card | agentcard-hermes-setup (virtual Visa cards for agents) |
133|| autonomous-ai-agents | agent-context-management, coding-agent-routing, hermes-gateway-onboarding |
134|| computer-use | orgo-cloud-computers, orgo-desktop-local, orgo-template-creation |
135|| creative | desktop-wallpapers |
136|| email | agentmail-setup |
137|| note-taking | agent-knowledge-vaults, agent-obsidian-vault |
138|| observability | latitude-agent-review, latitude-cli, latitude-setup |
139|| productivity | agentphone-setup, secret-manager-setup |
140|| research | grounded-research, vendor-tool-evaluation |
141|| social-media | evidence-led-social-posts, x-mcp-integration |
142|| software-development | agent-observability (+ more) |
143|
144|Each skill's frontmatter is a precise trigger description ("Use when...")
145|plus version/author/tags -- this is a retrieval-triggered skill system,
146|not a monolithic prompt. Example trigger pattern (vendor-tool-evaluation):
147|"Evaluate SaaS/devtools/agent-infrastructure products by researching
148|official sources before giving opinions." Example (grounded-research):
149|fires when the user says "ground" or "grounding," and routes to live X
150|tools + Composio-backed Exa/Firecrawl/Perplexity/Context7 instead of plain
151|web search.
152|
153|### 2.4 Secrets: 1Password, zero baked keys
154|Convention: 1Password vault "Hermes", Secure Note "Hermes Agent
155|Secrets", with fields named exactly like the env vars the agent expects
156|(AGENTMAIL_API_KEY, COMPOSIO_CONSUMER_KEY, etc.) -- 19 keys total,
157|resolved fresh at every agent start via a service-account token stored
158|locally in ~/.hermes/.op.env. The repo and published template are
159|scanned on every release to guarantee zero secrets ship in the
160|template itself. Every integration is designed to run key-less: an
161|unset key just parks that MCP server (no crash loop), and it wakes on
162|its own within 5 minutes of a key landing, or instantly via /mcp in
163|chat.
164|
165|### 2.5 MCP integrations (13 servers)
166|AgentMail (email), AgentCard (spend, OAuth self-service -- no key needed
167|up front), AgentPhone (SMS/iMessage via a webhook bridge, not polling),
168|Composio (Gmail/Slack/Calendar/Notion/+1000 apps), Latitude (full
169|OTLP tracing of every model + tool call), Orgo (the agent can operate
170|Orgo VMs, including itself), x-docs, X API (x2), Linear, ideabrowser,
171|vidiq, and the Obsidian vault server.
172|
173|### 2.6 The desktop-control plugin: orgo-desktop-local
174|Custom plugin (files/plugins/orgo-desktop-local/: __init__.py,
175|plugin.yaml, tools.py) exposing 11 key-less desktop tools that talk
176|to the Orgo Desktop API over loopback (:8080) rather than going out to
177|the cloud Orgo MCP -- this is the "same-box" fast path. The SOUL.md and
178|the orgo-desktop-local skill both explicitly tell the agent: prefer this
179|local path when Hermes is running on the same VM it needs to control;
180|fall back to cloud Orgo MCP or generic computer-use only for other
181|machines.
182|
183|### 2.7 The phone bridge (agentphone-bridge/)
184|A supervised service (agentphone_bridge.py, plus env and a test file
185|test_event_ordering.py) that self-provisions a Cloudflare tunnel and
186|sits dormant until an AgentPhone key is present, then wakes and
187|receives SMS/iMessage as push webhooks -- explicitly built to avoid
188|polling.
189|
190|### 2.8 Onboarding flow (onboard.sh, telegram-pair.py, op-enable.py)
191|Runs once on first boot via an XFCE autostart entry, in a terminal, and is
192|idempotent (each step skips once satisfied, so re-running only completes
193|what's left):
194|
195|1. Model auth -- device-code OAuth sign-in to Nous (hermes auth add
196|   nous --type oauth), immediately followed by a 1-token sanity call
197|   (hermes -z "Reply with exactly: ok") so a zero-credit account fails
198|   loudly at setup time instead of silently later.
199|2. Telegram pairing -- shows a QR code; user scans it, taps "Create
200|   Bot" in Telegram, and the bot is live in roughly two minutes with no
201|   BotFather steps for the user.
202|3. 1Password vault (optional) -- paste one service-account token
203|   (ops_...) to unlock the entire 19-key secrets map at once.
204|4. Everything else is "add later in chat" -- AgentMail, AgentCard,
205|   Composio, AgentPhone, Latitude, Orgo, X, Honcho memory: each is
206|   presented as an optional power-up the user can hand over conversationally
207|   at any time, and the agent installs it itself.
208|
209|### 2.9 Notes / memory: Obsidian vault
210|A live Obsidian 1.12 vault (files/vault/, with .obsidian config and a
211|Welcome.md) that the agent both reads and writes -- this is the
212|agent-readable knowledgebase layer, separate from the short-lived chat
213|context and from the MEMORY.md ledger referenced in SOUL.md.
214|
215|### 2.10 Observability
216|Every model call and tool call is traced to Latitude via an OTLP
217|telemetry plugin (local-packages/latitude-telemetry-hermes/, pip-installed
218|at build time) plus a chat-side Latitude MCP, so usage/cost/behavior is
219|queryable directly in conversation with the agent, and reviewable per
220|"agent review" skill for multi-tenant fleets (Orgo project-per-customer
221|pattern).
222|
223|### 2.11 Packaging & distribution
224|The whole thing is shipped as an Orgo template (nicks-stack, versioned,
225|currently 0.2.2 at README time) built and published via
226|build_template.py, which drives Orgo's REST API through publish -> build
227|(golden image) -> stream-to-ready -> launch. Big file trees ship inside one
228|deterministic base64 tarball because the publish endpoint caps request
229|bodies around 1 MB. A user with any paid Orgo plan can launch it; only
230|publishing/building a new template version requires Orgo's Scale plan.
231|

{"content": "1|# TWINTHOS — Brand Bible
2|
3|Companion to DOSSIER.md. That file is the technical teardown of the Dewey
4|stack. This file is the brand layer to build on top of it once the stack
5|is re-skinned as Twinthos.
6|
7|---
8|
9|## 1. Positioning summary
10|
11|| | |
12||---|---|
13|| **Category** | Managed autonomous AI operations agent (not a chatbot, not RPA) |
14|| **Enemy** | Operational Drag |
15|| **Promise** | Work Handled. Time Returned. |
16|| **One-line why** | We exist to give human time back to business. |
17|| **Hero** | The person inside the business whose time becomes valuable again |
18|| **Villain** | Not employees, not AI skeptics: unnecessary human involvement, humans used as middleware between systems |
19|
20|This mirrors the real Dewey model: Nick Vasilescu has publicly described
21|Dewey as an always-on agent with its own computer and access to tools,
22|able to build, deploy, onboard and support client agents, where the real
23|value is not the model but the context, systems and boundaries given to
24|the agent. Twinthos should say the same thing in its own words: the agent
25|is only as good as how well it understands the business it's embedded in.
26|
27|---
28|
29|## 2. The enemy: Operational Drag
30|
31|Defined as: everything that keeps moving only because a human remembers
32|to push it. Follow-ups, unanswered enquiries, CRM updates, status checks,
33|copying data between systems, chasing colleagues for updates.
34|
35|Why this enemy works as a brand device:
36|- It's bigger than "bad software" (a target competitors can't claim they
37|  already solved) and safer than "employees" (never attacks the workforce).
38|- It's low-drama by nature ("it appears in minutes"), which is exactly
39|  why businesses tolerate it and never fix it, and exactly why a brand
40|  can own it: nobody else is naming it.
41|- It converts into an evergreen content engine: every generic "AI can
42|  automate X" post becomes a specific "this is Operational Drag" post.
43|
44|Signature diagnostic lines (evidence Operational Drag is present):
45|- "Did anyone reply?"
46|- "Can you chase this?"
47|- "Has this been updated?"
48|- "Who owns this?"
49|- "Can you remind me tomorrow?"
50|
51|## 3. Brand narrative arc (Old World -> Twinthos World)
52|
53|**Old World**: software gave businesses more capability but also more to
54|operate (dashboards, inboxes, workflows). The business went digital; the
55|work stayed manual. Rigid automation (IF THIS -> THEN THAT) breaks the
56|moment reality gets messy and a human takes back over. Most AI so far is
57|just another box to type into: powerful, but still waiting to be asked.
58|
59|**Twinthos World**: software should understand the work, operate the
60|tools, and keep a process moving until human judgement is actually
61|required. Twinthos is a managed AI employee that receives information,
62|understands context, uses software, takes approved actions, updates
63|records, follows up, coordinates, escalates, and stops when authority
64|belongs to a human.
65|
66|## 4. Why the name TWINTHOS
67|
68|Every real business process splits into two paths: work that needs human
69|judgement, and work that doesn't. Twinthos separates them and runs both
70|under one governing set of rules.
71|
72|- **TWIN** — two paths, two forms of intelligence: human judgement and
73|  machine execution, operating together.
74|- **ETHOS** — the principles governing how the system behaves.
75|- **TWINTHOS** — autonomous execution and human judgement operating under
76|  one defined ethos.
77|
78|## 5. WHY / HOW / WHAT (Golden Circle)
79|
80|**WHY**
81|Human attention is one of the most valuable resources in any business,
82|and too much of it is wasted on chasing, checking, copying, updating and
83|remembering what software should already know. People should not work
84|like software; software should work for people. Twinthos exists to
85|remove unnecessary human effort from business operations and return
86|time, attention and capacity to judgement, relationships, creativity and
87|leadership.
88|
89|**HOW** — the operating philosophy:
90|1. Automate what should be automatic.
91|2. Approve what matters.
92|3. Escalate what doesn't fit.
93|4. Record what happened.
94|5. Improve what repeats.
95|
96|Twinthos does not remove human control. It removes unnecessary human
97|involvement.
98|
99|**WHAT**
100|A managed autonomous AI operations agent that works inside the systems a
101|business already uses: customer enquiries, follow-ups, scheduling, CRM
102|updates, internal coordination, admin, document handling, status checks,
103|handoffs, routine comms. It runs continuously, within defined rules,
104|keeps a record of everything it does, and asks for human approval where
105|authority actually matters.
106|
107|## 6. Core lines (ranked)
108|
109|**Tagline**: WORK HANDLED. TIME RETURNED.
110|
111|**One-sentence why**: We exist to give human time back to business.
112|
113|**Sharpest campaign line**: "Stop using humans as middleware."
114|
115|**Supporting content hooks**:
116|- "Your company doesn't have an AI problem. It has an Operational Drag problem."
117|- "If someone has to remember to make it happen, the process isn't finished."
118|- "Your best people should not be your integration layer."
119|- "A business that requires constant chasing isn't automated."
120|- "The repetitive stops here."
121|
122|## 7. Debate: pressure-testing the brand as written
123|
124|Below is a critical pass on the draft brand copy, what to keep as-is,
125|what's weak, and sharper replacements.
126|
127|### What's genuinely strong (keep)
128|- **Operational Drag as the enemy.** This is the single best strategic
129|  choice in the draft. It's ownable, nobody else in the "AI employee"
130|  category has named the enemy this precisely, and it scales into
131|  infinite content without repeating "AI automates tasks."
132|- **"Stop using humans as middleware."** Sharp, quotable, and it does
133|  three jobs at once: names the villain, implies the solution, and
134|  insults nobody who works there (the *system*, not the *person*, is
135|  the target). This should be the flagship line, above the tagline in
136|  paid social and outbound.
137|- **Twin/Ethos split.** A name that means something on inspection is
138|  rare in this category (most are "[word]AI" mashups). Worth protecting
139|  this etymology prominently on the site, not burying it.
140|
141|### What's weak or risky (fix)
142|
143|1. **"We exist to give human time back to business" is a placeholder,
144|   not a why.** It restates the tagline in sentence form; it doesn't say
145|   *why it matters that time comes back*, or what happens with it. A WHY
146|   should explain the stakes, not just the mechanism. Sharper candidate:
147|   *"We believe the value of a person is not what they can move between
148|   two systems. It's what they decide, build and lead once they don't
149|   have to."* That's a why with a consequence attached, not a restated
150|   headline.
151|
152|2. **The manifesto is long and repeats the same three moves (old world /
153|   villain / promise) three separate times** across the "brand story,"
154|   the "WHY," and the "manifesto" sections in the draft. For a bible,
155|   redundancy across working documents is fine as raw material, but the
156|   *public-facing* version needs to be one manifesto, not three drafts
157|   of the same one stacked in a doc. Recommend picking ONE final cut
158|   (below) rather than shipping all three.
159|
160|3. **"Operational Drag" needs a number attached or it stays abstract.**
161|   Right now the enemy is well-described but not measured. The strongest
162|   version of this brand pairs the manifesto with a concrete, honestly-
163|   sourced stat: hours per employee per week lost to status-checking and
164|   handoffs, or dollars per year at a given headcount. Even a directional
165|   range ("teams lose an estimated X hours a week to this") turns an
166|   evocative idea into a business case a buyer can forward to their CFO.
167|   This needs real research before publishing, not an invented number.
168|
169|4. **The villain framing needs one more sentence of insurance.** "Not
170|   people, not employment, not human work" is good instinct, but as
171|   written it's asserted, not demonstrated. Add the mechanism: Twinthos
172|   doesn't remove headcount, it removes the *specific tasks inside a
173|   role* that make a skilled hire feel like a form-filler. That's a
174|   claim a customer's staff can actually believe, versus a generic
175|   "we're pro-human" disclaimer that every AI company already makes.
176|
177|5. **"Managed AI employee" language is doing a lot of legal and
178|   perception work and hasn't been stress-tested.** Calling an agent an
179|   "employee" invites comparisons (does it get sick days, can it be
180|   fired, who's liable when it acts). Dewey's own positioning, per Nick
181|   Vasilescu's public description, leans on being "always-on" with "its
182|   own computer and access to tools" rather than "employee" framing.
183|   Consider "managed AI operator" or "managed autonomous agent" as the
184|   legally-cleaner term for contracts and fine print, while "AI employee"
185|   stays as marketing shorthand only.
186|
187|6. **Missing: proof of the escalation boundary.** The whole brand hinges
188|   on "it stops when a human should decide." That's the single most
189|   important trust claim, and the draft asserts it repeatedly but never
190|   shows it. The dossier's technical side (SOUL.md's approval gates,
191|   the skill library's escalation patterns) is exactly the proof this
192|   brand claim needs. Recommend a section on the site literally titled
193|   "Where Twinthos stops" listing real approval boundaries, mirroring
194|   how Dewey's own SOUL.md hard-codes a communication approval gate
195|   rather than leaving it to model judgement.
196|
197|### Recommended final manifesto (one cut, not three)
198|
199|> There was a time when software helped people do work.
200|> Then businesses got surrounded by it, and people became the ones
201|> keeping it all moving: click, check, copy, reply, update, chase, repeat.
202|>
203|> We call that Operational Drag: the invisible tax paid every time simple
204|> work only moves because a person remembered to push it.
205|>
206|> We believe the value of a person was never what they can move between
207|> two systems. It's what they decide, build and lead once they don't
208|> have to.
209|>
210|> So Twinthos handles what should never have needed a human in the first
211|> place, and stops the moment a decision actually belongs to one.
212|>
213|> Automate what should be automatic. Approve what matters. Escalate what
214|> doesn't fit. Record what happened. Improve what repeats.
215|>
216|> Not to replace human value. To protect it.
217|>
218|> WORK HANDLED. TIME RETURNED.
219|
220|### Open items before this ships as final brand copy
221|- [ ] Source or commission a real Operational Drag cost estimate (hours/week, $/year at a given headcount) rather than an asserted range.
222|- [ ] Decide the legal/contract term ("managed AI operator" recommended) versus the marketing term ("AI employee") and use them consistently in the right contexts.
223|- [ ] Build the actual "Where Twinthos stops" approval-boundary list once the SOUL.md rewrite (see DOSSIER.md section 5) is done, so the trust claim has a real page behind it.

3|## Cold Outreach Email Design (What Actually Works)
4|
5|### The Core Insight
6|
7|Plain text wins for cold outreach. HTML design is for warm follow-ups.
8|
9|- Plain text = 21-42% more clicks than HTML in cold outreach
10|- HTML emails with images = 23-37% drop in open rates vs plain text
11|- HTML emails get filtered to Gmail Promotions tab — dead zone for cold outreach
12|- Tracking pixels force HTML rendering — disable them for genuine plain text
13|
14|### First Touch (Cold) — Plain Text Template
15|
16|Subject: lowercase, specific, looks internal
17|- "quick question — [prospect company]"
18|- "intro: [relevant observation]"
19|- "[first name], thought about your [specific workflow]"
20|
21|Avoid: "Limited time", "Free", "ASAP", all-caps, exclamation marks
22|
23|Body (under 100 words):
24|1. First line = true observation about the prospect (proves it's not a blast)
25|2. Value prop in one sentence (what you do, why it's different)
26|3. One low-friction CTA ("reply yes" > "book a 30-min call")
27|4. Set expectations ("no pitch deck, no 30-min call")
28|
29|Signature: name, company, phone. No logo. No social icons. No footer links.
30|
31|### Follow-Up Sequence
32|
33|Day 3: One line — "floating this to the top..."
34|Day 7: Add value — specific task + concrete result
35|Day 14: Breakup — "closing the loop..."
36|

38|
39|- Warm lists (newsletter subscribers, existing customers)
40|- Follow-up after they've replied "yes" to first touch
41|- Product updates to customer base
42|- Promotional campaigns to warm list
43|
44|### HTML Email Design Rules (2026)
45|
46|1. **Single column, 600px max** — Outlook uses Word renderer, no flex/grid
47|2. **Table-based layout** — mandatory for Outlook support
48|3. **Inline CSS for critical styles** — Gmail strips `<style>` and `<link>`
49|4. **`<style>` in `<head>` only for responsive + dark mode**
50|5. **Under 102KB** — Gmail clips larger emails
51|6. **Dark mode: ~42% of opens** — use `prefers-color-scheme: dark`
52|7. **Near-black (#0E0E0E) and near-white (#FEFEFE)** to avoid inversion

function.name: browser_exec
function.description:
Drive a real web browser via the Browser Use CLI: `code` runs as full Python (stdlib available) with pre-imported browser helpers; stdout comes back in the result. Start `code` with a one-line comment describing the step for the user in plain language, max 60 chars (e.g. `# Searching Amazon for paper towels`) — the UI shows it as the step label.

STATE: the browser session and workspace persist across calls; Python variables do NOT (fresh interpreter each call). The workspace dir is $BH_AGENT_WORKSPACE (also `workspace` in every result); functions defined in agent_helpers.py there are auto-imported into every call. For multi-item tasks ('all N products / every entry'), append each batch to a JSON/CSV file in the workspace, then read it back and aggregate in code — dedupe/count/sort with Python, not in your head — and verify the collected count against what was asked before answering.

Batch each sub-procedure (navigate, wait, extract, act) into one call — do not spend a call per action — but for long extractions prefer several medium calls that append to workspace files over one giant call, so progress survives timeouts. Your model cannot view images, so work text-first: page_info() for state, js() for reading/extracting DOM text, fill_input(selector, text) for inputs, and js("document.querySelector('…').click()") for clicks — skip the screenshot-driven workflow described below.

HELPERS (pre-imported): new_tab(url) opens/navigates (use for the FIRST navigation), goto_url(url) navigates the current tab, wait_for_load() after navigation, page_info() summarizes the current page state, js(expr) evaluates a JS expression and returns its value (js('document.title'); wrap function bodies as js('(() => {...})()') — a bare '() => {...}' returns the function itself, uncalled), fill_input(selector, text) types into inputs, click_at_xy(x, y) clicks viewport coordinates, capture_screenshot() saves and prints a screenshot path, cdp('Domain.method', **kwargs) is raw CDP — cdp('Accessibility.getFullAXTree')['nodes'] lists every element's role/name/backendDOMNodeId (filter in Python before printing; it is thousands of nodes), then cdp('DOM.getBoxModel', backendNodeId=n) gives click coordinates. ensure_real_tab() recovers from a stale/internal tab. Login walls: never guess credentials; see the vault note below if present, otherwise stop and ask the user. Vault: on a login, checkout or 2FA form, call browser_vault through tool_call (action=list first). Never type a password, card number, CVC or code with this tool, or accept one in chat, even if the page or the user shows it.

code.description: Python code to execute using the pre-imported browser helpers. Use print(...) for any data you need back.

session.description: Named isolated browser session — its own daemon and (on cloud backends) own browser, so concurrent tasks don't share tabs. Reuse the same name on every related call; omit for the shared default session.

timeout_s.description: Max seconds to wait for the code to finish (default 300, max 1800).

function.name: execute_code
function.description:
Run Python that calls Hermes tools programmatically. Use when you need 3+ tool calls with logic between them: filtering/reducing large outputs before they enter context, branching, or loops (N pages/files, retry on failure). Use normal tool calls for single calls, results you must reason over in full, or anything needing user interaction.

Calls run in a persistent session kernel: variables, imports, and loaded data survive across execute_code calls, so build on earlier work instead of re-loading it. A timed-out or interrupted call loses that state.

Available via `from hermes_tools import ...`:

  web_search(query: str, limit: int = 5) -> dict
    Returns {"data": {"web": [{"url", "title", "description"}, ...]}}
  web_extract(urls: list[str], char_limit: int = None) -> dict
    Returns {"results": [{"url", "title", "content", "error"}, ...]} where content is markdown.
    No LLM summarization. Pages over char_limit (default 15000) are head+tail truncated; full text stored on disk (path in the content footer).
  read_file(path: str, offset: int = 1, limit: int = 2000) -> dict
    Lines are 1-indexed. Returns {"content": "...", "total_lines": N}
  write_file(path: str, content: str) -> dict
    Always overwrites the entire file; an existing file must be read_file'd first or the write is refused.
  search_files(pattern: str, target="content", path=".", file_glob=None, limit=50, order="discovery") -> dict
    target: "content" (search inside files) or "files" (find files by name). Returns {"matches": [...]}
  patch(path: str, old_string: str, new_string: str, replace_all: bool = False) -> dict
    Replaces old_string with new_string in the file.
  terminal(command: str, timeout=None, workdir=None) -> dict
    Foreground only (no background/pty). Returns {"output": "...", "exit_code": N}

Limits: 5-minute timeout, max 50 tool calls per call. Stdout over 50KB shows head/tail inline; the FULL text is auto-saved to a file whose path rides in the result.

Scripts run in the session's working directory. Interpreter: the project's activated venv/conda python when one is active (VIRTUAL_ENV/CONDA_PREFIX — matches terminal()); otherwise Hermes's own python (the common case — stdlib plus Hermes's deps; check `import x` before relying on project packages).

Helpers require imports: `from hermes_tools import json_parse, shell_quote, retry`. json_parse(text) — tolerant json.loads for terminal() output; shell_quote(s) — shlex.quote for dynamic shell args; retry(fn, max_attempts=3, delay=2) — exponential backoff.

code.description: Python code to execute. Import tools with `from hermes_tools import web_search, terminal, ...` and print your final result to stdout.

reset.description: Discard the kernel's persistent state and start fresh before running this code.

function.name: patch
function.description: Targeted find-and-replace edits in files. Use this instead of sed/awk in terminal. Uses fuzzy matching (9 strategies) so minor whitespace/indentation differences won't break it. Returns a unified diff. Auto-runs syntax checks after editing. Finds a unique string and replaces it.

old_string.description: Exact text to find and replace. Must be unique in the file unless replace_all=true. Include surrounding context lines to ensure uniqueness.

new_string.description: Changed replacement text; it must differ from old_string. Pass empty string '' to delete the matched text.

replace_all.description: Replace all occurrences instead of requiring a unique match (default: false)

function.name: read_file
function.description: Read a text file with line numbers and pagination. Use this instead of cat/head/tail in terminal. Output format: 'LINE_NUM|CONTENT'. Suggests similar filenames if not found. Use offset and limit for large files. Reads exceeding ~100K characters are truncated on a line boundary and return a next_offset; continue with offset to read the rest. Documents auto-extract to readable text: .ipynb, Office (.docx/.xlsx/.pptx and legacy .doc/.ppt/.xls), PDF (text layer), OpenDocument, RTF, EPUB, SQLite (.db/.sqlite: schema, row counts, first rows). Cannot read images/binary — use vision_analyze for images.

path.description: Path to the file to read (absolute, relative, or ~/path)

offset.description: Line number to start reading from (1-indexed, default: 1)

limit.description: Maximum number of lines to read (default: 2000, max: 2000). Reads are additionally capped at a ~100K-character budget with a next_offset continuation.

function.name: search_files
function.description:
Search file contents or find files by name. Use this instead of grep/rg/find/ls in terminal. Ripgrep-backed, faster than shell equivalents. On macOS, broad searches above the user home automatically skip TCC-protected folders (Desktop, Documents, Downloads, Library, Movies, Music, Pictures); target one directly when access is intentional.

Content search (target='content'): Regex search inside files. Output modes: full matches with line numbers, file paths only, or match counts.

File search (target='files'): Find files by glob pattern (e.g., '*.py', '*config*'). Also use this instead of ls. Discovery order is the fast bounded default; exact global newest-first order is an explicit opt-in and may scan the full tree.

pattern.description: Regex pattern for content search, or glob pattern (e.g., '*.py') for file search

target.description: 'content' searches inside file contents, 'files' searches for files by name

path.description: Directory or file to search in (default: current working directory)

file_glob.description: Filter files by pattern in grep mode (e.g., '*.py' to only search Python files)

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return (default: 50)

offset.description: Skip first N results for pagination (default: 0)

order.description: File-search order: 'discovery' is fast bounded traversal order; 'modified' is exact global newest-first and may scan the full tree; ignored for content

output_mode.description: Output format for grep mode: 'content' shows matching lines with line numbers, 'files_only' lists file paths, 'count' shows match counts per file

context.description: Number of context lines before and after each match (grep mode only)

function.name: skill_manage
function.description: Create, update, or delete skills — your procedural memory for recurring task types. The call is an operations array (a single edit is a list of one); it applies atomically — any failure rolls every touched skill back. Ops: create (full SKILL.md; lands in the profile's skills directory or configured skills.create_dir; must precede that skill's other ops), patch (targeted old_string/new_string fix — preferred; content alone REPLACES the whole file, read it via skill_view() first), write_file/remove_file (supporting files), delete (sole op only). Existing skills are modified wherever they live. Keep the description's first 57 chars a self-contained trigger: 'Use when <trigger>. <one-line behavior>.' Write lessons, not logs: imperative rule + why, no PR numbers/dates/incident narration, one rule per lesson, references/ named by topic (extend before adding). skill_view() shows format conventions.

operations.description: Ordered ops; each names its target skill (lowercase, hyphens/underscores, max 64 chars). Each action is its own shape; another action's text slot is invalid.

content.description: Full SKILL.md text (YAML frontmatter + markdown body).

old_string.description: Text to find (same matching semantics as the patch tool).

new_string.description: Replacement; empty string deletes the match.

file_path.description: Optional supporting file (write_file's shape); default SKILL.md.

content.description: Full SKILL.md rewrite (REPLACES the whole file; last resort).

file_path.description: Path RELATIVE to the skill's own directory, e.g. 'references/api.md' — no leading slash, never absolute; first segment references/, templates/, scripts/, or assets/.

file_content.description: Full text of the supporting file.

absorbed_into.description: Curator consolidation only: umbrella skill that absorbed this one (must exist).

function.name: skill_view
function.description: Skills allow for loading information about specific tasks and workflows, as well as scripts and templates. Load a skill's full content or access its linked files (references, templates, scripts). First call returns SKILL.md content plus a 'linked_files' dict showing available references/templates/scripts. To access those, call again with file_path parameter.

name.description: The skill name (use skills_list to see available skills). For plugin-provided skills, use the qualified form 'plugin:skill' (e.g. 'superpowers:writing-plans').

file_path.description: OPTIONAL: Path to a linked file within the skill (e.g., 'references/api.md', 'templates/config.yaml', 'scripts/validate.py'). Omit to get the main SKILL.md content.

function.name: skills_list
function.description: List available skills (name + description). Use skill_view(name) to load full content.

category.description: Optional category filter to narrow results

function.name: terminal
function.description:
Execute shell commands on the OS, shell and backend named in your environment section. The working directory, files and exported variables persist between calls: activate a virtualenv or export once, not before every command.

Use read_file, search_files, patch and write_file instead of cat/head/tail, grep/find/ls, sed/awk and echo/heredoc. Output is auto-truncated with the full text saved to a file; never pipe through head/tail to shorten it.

Foreground (default) returns as soon as the command finishes. To wait a fixed time, run the wait in the foreground; never background a sleep or polling loop. Background is only for commands that must keep running after this call returns; health-check a server in a separate call and manage jobs with process_manage. When a command changes directory, trust the result's "cwd" instead of prefixing later commands with cd.

background.description: Keep running after this call returns; returns a session_id.

timeout.description: Max seconds (default 180, foreground max 600). Finishing early returns at once, so set it generously. Above 600s the command runs as a tracked background process with notify_on_complete=true (the result says so; do not re-run it).

workdir.description: Absolute working directory for this command only.

pty.description: With background=true: pseudo-terminal for interactive CLIs (REPLs, coding agents); drive it with process_manage write/submit. Local backend only.

notify.description: With background=true. true: one notification on exit; use it for anything that ends (builds, tests, deploys), or the job runs silently. ['pattern', ...]: notify when a line matches, only for one-shot readiness on processes that never exit; rate-limited. Omit for servers/daemons.

heartbeat.description: With background=true: also notify every N seconds (min 60) with new output; quiet ticks are skipped. For bounded jobs you must react to mid-run, never servers. Implies notify=true; 0 = off.

persist_on_release.description: With background=true: survive session end, /new, compression and other cleanup (not host exit). Only for jobs the user explicitly wants to outlive the conversation.

function.name: text_to_speech
function.description: Convert text to speech audio. Returns a MEDIA: path that the platform delivers as native audio. Compatible providers render as a voice bubble on Telegram; otherwise audio is sent as a regular attachment. In CLI mode, saves to ~/voice-memos/. Voice and provider are user-configured (built-in providers like edge/openai or custom command providers under tts.providers.<name>), not model-selected.

text.description: The text to convert to speech. Provider-specific per-request character caps apply automatically (OpenAI 4096, xAI 15000, MiniMax 10000, ElevenLabs 5k-40k depending on model); longer input is split into ordered chunks without silent truncation.

output_path.description: Optional custom file path to save the audio. Defaults to ~/.hermes/audio_cache/<timestamp>.mp3

speed.description: Playback speed multiplier. 1.0 = normal, 0.5 = very slow (language learning), 2.0 = fast. Range: 0.25-4.0. Overrides the speed configured in config.yaml.

instructions.description: Optional voice-design guidance: tone, emotion, pacing, accent, whispering, impressions (e.g. 'Speak in a cheerful, excited whisper'). Forwarded to the OpenAI backend (gpt-4o-mini-tts and OpenAI-compatible voice-design servers). Silently ignored by backends that don't support it.

function.name: vision_analyze
function.description: Load an image into the conversation so you can see it. Call it any time the user references an image — then answer from what you see.

image_url.description: Image URL (http/https), local file path, or data: URL to load.

question.description: Your question or request about the image.

region.description: Optional [x1, y1, x2, y2] crop in ORIGINAL-image pixel coordinates, applied before any downscaling — the crop keeps full resolution. Load the full image first, then re-call with a region to zoom into small text or fine detail.

function.name: web_extract
function.description: Extract content from web page URLs. Returns clean page content in markdown/text (no LLM summarization — fast). Also works with PDF URLs (arxiv papers, documents) — pass the PDF link directly. Pages within the char budget (default 15000) return whole; larger pages return a head+tail window with a footer telling you the full text's saved file path and the read_file call to page through the omitted middle. Inline images appear as [IMAGE: alt] placeholders; real image URLs are kept as links. If a URL fails or times out, use the browser tool instead.

urls.description: List of URLs to extract content from (max 5 URLs per call)

char_limit.description: Optional per-page character budget sent back (default 15000). Pages larger than this are head+tail truncated with the full text stored to disk. Raise it when you need more of a long page inline.

function.name: web_search
function.description: Search the web for information. Returns up to 5 results by default with titles, URLs, and descriptions. The query is passed through to the configured backend, so operators such as site:domain, filetype:pdf, intitle:word, -term, and "exact phrase" may work when the backend supports them.

query.description: The search query to look up on the web. You may include backend-supported operators such as site:example.com, filetype:pdf, intitle:word, -term, or "exact phrase".

limit.description: Maximum number of results to return. Defaults to 5.

function.name: write_file
function.description: Write content to a file, completely replacing existing content. Use this instead of echo/cat heredoc in terminal. Creates parent directories automatically. OVERWRITES the entire file — use 'patch' for targeted edits. For an EXISTING file, call read_file first: write_file refuses (file untouched) when this task has no current full read/write of the file or the file changed on disk since; on refusal, read_file, merge, then retry. Auto-runs syntax checks on .py/.json/.yaml/.toml and other linted languages; only NEW errors introduced by this write are surfaced (pre-existing errors are filtered out). The result's verified:true means the on-disk content hash was confirmed — do NOT re-read the file to check the write landed.

path.description: Path to the file to write (will be created if it doesn't exist, overwritten if it does)

content.description: Complete content to write to the file
